questions.q: What is the 'friction vs. identity confidence' trade-off?
options: It only applies to internal employee logins, never customers
It describes the trade-off between SAML and OIDC specifically
There is no such trade-off; more friction always improves everything with no downside
Adding verification steps increases confidence a user is who they claim to be, but also increases signup/login abandonment
questions.explain: Every added friction point (password rules, MFA, manual verification) raises identity confidence at the cost of higher abandonment — there's no setting that maximizes both at once.

questions.q: What does centralizing identity in a hub-and-spoke IdP model risk, even though it improves consistency?
options: A hub outage or compromise can affect every downstream application at once, and individual apps lose autonomy over their own login rules
It makes MFA impossible to enforce
It eliminates the need for any authentication at all
Nothing; centralization has no downside
questions.explain: Centralizing control in one hub concentrates risk — an outage or compromise there has a much wider blast radius than a single app's independent authentication failing.

questions.q: Why might a real organization stay on a legacy mechanism like delegated authentication or the Legacy Named Credential schema, even knowing a modern alternative exists?
options: Salesforce forces all orgs to keep legacy mechanisms permanently
Legacy mechanisms are always technically superior
Migrating away carries engineering time and cutover risk that has to be weighed against the ongoing cost of staying on the legacy path
Modern alternatives are never actually better
questions.explain: The trade-off is the one-time cost and risk of migrating versus the ongoing cost of remaining on the legacy approach — not a simple case of the modern option being free to adopt.

questions.q: What accountability trade-off does choosing Named Principal over Per-User create?
options: Per-User is always simpler to configure than Named Principal
Named Principal provides stronger per-user audit trails than Per-User
None; the two are functionally identical
Named Principal is simpler to configure but loses the ability for the external system to distinguish which individual Salesforce user triggered each call
questions.explain: Named Principal's simplicity comes at the cost of collapsing every user's outbound activity into one shared identity, which defeats any per-user accountability the external system might otherwise support.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is usually the architect's actual job when facing an identity design trade-off?
options: To surface the trade-off explicitly so the client makes an informed choice, stating what they gain and what they give up
To always default to whichever option is cheapest to implement
To hide the downside so the client feels more confident in the decision
To eliminate the trade-off entirely so the client never has to choose
questions.explain: Since most of these trade-offs are structurally impossible to eliminate, the architect's real job is to make sure the client understands what they're gaining and giving up before committing to a direction.
